maintopic: WHEAT-REPORTED AGREEMENT ON FREE WORLD MARKET AFTER JULY 31

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: WHEAT-REPORTED AGREEMENT ON FREE WORLD MARKET AFTER JULY 31
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I desire to direct a question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce regarding press reports to the effect that at the meeting in London the wheat importing and exporting countries have agreed by majority
decision that after July 31 importing countries will not be required to take a prearranged minimum quantity of wheat, and there will be no predetermined price range.
Since this was a majority decision I take it there was some disagreement. I should like to ask the minister what position the Canadian delegation took, whether Canada voted in favour of this free market after July 31, and whether this is the government's policy with respect to this matter.

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert Winters (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
maintopic: WHEAT-REPORTED AGREEMENT ON FREE WORLD MARKET AFTER JULY 31
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker. As I mentioned yesterday and as I have said on previous occasions, our major effort is being made through negotiations for a new cereals agreement presently in progress at Geneva. At Geneva we have been seeking a substantially increased price for wheat and an increased price range. Under the circumstances we are unwilling to agree to a continuation of the price and the price range as provided for under the present international wheat agreement. So all we would agree to in the London discussion was a continuation of the framework of the agreement, but not the price structure.

maintopic: WHEAT-REPORTED AGREEMENT ON FREE WORLD MARKET AFTER JULY 31
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in view of the fact that the negotiations in Geneva are not likely to be concluded before the beginning of the new crop year, do I take it that at the London meeting the government voted to have a free market after July 31, and to remove the protective provisions which are contained in the present international wheat agreement?

maintopic: WHEAT-REPORTED AGREEMENT ON FREE WORLD MARKET AFTER JULY 31
speechtext:
Under the terms of the negotiations at Geneva they must be concluded by mid-year, so it is entirely likely that the present arrangements under the international wheat agreement will be succeeded by new arrangements under a cereals agreement as part of the Kennedy round of negotiations. So anything that is being done in London now does not in any way commit us to a price structure or a marketing arrangement; it simply keeps in being the framework of the I.W.A. and no more.

subtopic: PROTECTION OF U.S. VICE PRESIDENT ON CANADIAN VISIT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to address a question to the Solicitor General. My question is based on criticism and considerable annoyance expressed by some Canadians and in newspaper editorials with respect to the necessity for two carloads of F.B.I. men to come to Canada to protect United States Vice President Hubert Humphrey on his recent visit to Canada.
My question is this. Will the minister inform the house whether in his opinion it was necessary for the F.B.I. to come to Canada on this occasion? subtopic: PROTECTION OF U.S. VICE PRESIDENT ON CANADIAN VISIT

subtopic: PROTECTION OF U.S. VICE PRESIDENT ON CANADIAN VISIT

subtopic: PROTECTION OF U.S. VICE PRESIDENT ON CANADIAN VISIT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I cannot accept as a fact the preliminary part of the question. I will say, however, that the R.C.M.P. are co-operating closely with law enforcement agencies in the United States to keep crime under control.

subtopic: PROTECTION OF U.S. VICE PRESIDENT ON CANADIAN VISIT
speechtext: I ask specifically whether at this very moment and in the last week there have been meetings between the R.C.M.P. and United States officials of the F.B.I. and the like, to prevent or do something to prevent the influx into Montreal and Toronto of United States mafia figures.

April 7. 1967

municipal officials who were visiting New York state.

subtopic: PROTECTION OF U.S. VICE PRESIDENT ON CANADIAN VISIT
speechtext: I am referring to the New York Times, which refers to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.

speechtext:

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it is not my intention to pursue much further the few comments I made yesterday as to the inaccuracy of the statement by the Secretary of State for External Affairs concerning the confidence which the House of Commons should have in the Minister of National Defence. Today I intend to proceed with a few general comments as to what the position is in this chamber now with respect to this bill, particularly in view of the apparent confusion in the mind of the hon. member for Keno-ra-Rainy River, and in the minds of some other hon. members as to what are the issues before us that we should consider.
First, of course, I am aware that we are in the awkward position that the house gave this bill second reading and then held committee hearings to determine whether the house should pass the question of unification in principle. Having held many committee hearings and having had the benefit of the advice of the best and most senior military minds in Canada, most of whom unfortunately were prematurely dumped by this amateur minister, I think we should now consider the evidence we have obtained. We must approach this on the basis of the evidence itself, the credibility of the witnesses, their experience and the sum total of all evidence on each point that may be in issue when we are considering whether we should adopt any clause of this bill on unification.
There was much comment in the House of Commons and in the defence committee, while we were trying to get more witnesses who could give more valuable information, to the effect that we had heard enough witnesses. I heard Liberal members on the defence committee suggest that we were getting one for one on each side, and that it seemed to be balancing out.
Liberal members seemed to have the feeling that if they could call one witness from within the Department of National Defence who would follow the minister's instructions, this would balance off the testimony of another witness who had the freedom to speak and give that committee the benefit of his experience and knowledge as one who had no motive
[Mr. Plckersglll.l
but his own wish to assist his country by expressing his views. Those witnesses called who were no longer in the department were motivated only by a desire to bring to the attention of the committee all the facts and information and knowledge they had accumulated, the benefit of their years of experience and wisdom, so that we in the House of Commons and in the defence committee might be in a better position to judge the facts and decide on the basis of expert military testimony what was best for us to do with this bill.
Having pointed out the position of those people, and having mentioned the position of the Liberals on the defence committee-that it was a case of one from each side-I think we should now refer to the evidence of General Allard, particularly his opening statement which gives the House of Commons its most valuable indication as to the strength of the evidence presented by various people. If my hon. friends on my right would continue their conversations behind the curtain, Mr. Chairman, perhaps I could make myself heard in this chamber.
We first became aware of how difficult this problem was in the Landymore incident when I charged the minister with tampering with the evidence. You will recall that at that time the minister said or gave the impression that he felt that because this witness was a serving officer responsible to the minister he, the minister, had the right to review his evidence; that the witness was appearing as a representative of the minister; that that made the minister responsible for his evidence and therefore that was the only kind of evidence that could be given. I believe each witness who has appeared from the defence department has believed in this course of conduct. I believe that if a serving officer feels-

Considering the behavior of the Minister of National Defence concerning those under his power and the way in which he has treated them, I consider the minister the oddest source from which any appeal to human decency can come. Not only that, Mr. Chairman; it is I think evident from the remarks I have made-and if the minister will allow me to continue-that I have been very fair to those individuals. I have not suggested in any way for one minute that any one of them has lied to the committee. What I have suggested is that they had a duty to the department-and that is the way they seemed to believe it-to give to the committee that viewpoint which represents official departmental thinking, and that they are not permitted to say otherwise.
Certainly the Admiral Landymore case was a classic example. The minister changed the testimony. Admiral Landymore, being duty bound to follow the advice of his minister, found himself unable to challenge the authority of the minister to do this because he had to be guided as to the authority of the minister by the minister himself. But that did not stop him from feeling resentment and later on, when he was attacked by the minister, revealing the facts.
National Defence Act Amendment [DOT] (11:50 a.m.)
I was going to quote from the testimony of General Allard who gave us a very clear warning as to the limitation on his ability to speak before the committee. This quotation appears in volume 27 of the minutes of proceedings and evidence of the standing committee on national defence at page 1759. I shall read the whole paragraph because I think it is worthy of consideration by this house in respect of the credibility, importance and weight that should be placed on the evidence given by various witnesses. General Allard said this:
It is with mixed feelings that I appear before you today. I say this because although I know this will make no difference to the prerogatives and privileges of this committee-nor should it-I personally think that some of the practices and methods of operation are paradoxical. On the one hand, there are called before you officers of the forces, like myself, who are responsible for the organization, efficiency, and morale of the forces for your defence, and who can speak only within the bounds of these responsibilities under the policies set forth by the government.
Perhaps I should repeat that last sentence, because it represents in essence the attitude taken by General Allard and the other witnesses from the defence department who appeared before the committee. It gives us a clear indication of the limitation on their evidence and the extent to which we are able to find out the personal feelings of those testifying. Let me repeat the last sentence, or the last part of it:
-who can speak only within the bounds of these reponsibilities under the policies set forth by the government.
General Allard then continued:
On the other hand, other people are called before you, who have no responsibilities to anybody but themselves, and therefore can make statements on matters for which they bear no responsibility.
I pointed out to General Allard at the time that as a gentleman he might like to change those last words by saying instead of "no responsibility", responsibility only as to themselves on their honour as gentlemen and former officers. If we ever lose sight of this limitation on the ability of serving officers to speak when assessing the evidence given before the committee we will fail to recognize the value of that evidence.
General Allard gave a clear warning in that statement. That is quite different to what the minister said I was suggesting, that officers were not being honest before the committee. The general's statement indicates that he has gone as far as he can to tell the committee
April 7, 1967

National Defence Act Amendment how his evidence must be read. The treatment of Landymore is an indication of how careful we must be in reading the evidence of those witnesses who are under the thumb and direction of the minister. The minister's attitude has been consistent in this regard. I suppose he still feels he had the right to tamper with the evidence of the witnesses, to keep witnesses from giving their own personal opinions and to restrict them to giving the official party line.
I still contend that he has no right to do that. General Allard has told us clearly and simply that he accepts the minister's direction in this regard. It is my submission that if the chief of staff accepts that direction, then every officer under him and the minister must accept it. For that reason the skill and experience of an officer who has given testimony is of assistance to us only in understanding his technical knowledge and thorough appreciation of his department's work. The evidence gives us no clue whatsoever as to the personal feelings or beliefs of those officers who testify.
In view of the clear warning given us by General Allard I submit we do not obtain his personal opinion at all from the answers he gives to questions regarding the practicability of unification and whether it will work. He indicated that his job when testifying was to present official government policy. Therefore it was his duty to answer in the terms he did. In support of this submission I suggest we have the testimony of others, including retired officers, to the effect that as long as they maintained their positions they had to accept direction. They have said that when they found they could no longer go along with policy they had to resign. For this reason the first lesson to be learned from the committee hearings is how the evidence must be weighed.
The suggestion by members on the Liberal side that the evidence of one group of officers to the effect that unification will work balances the evidence of the other group who said it will not work is pure nonsense. The only indication we have had that unification is good has come in statements put into the mouths of certain officers by the Minister of National Defence. In my submission those statements are completely worthless as evidence. Therefore the only statements we can count on as representing the experience and honest opinions of the gentlemen giving evidence are those statements of the officers who were in a position to speak freely and honestly without restriction and without fear of

reprisal. Those gentlemen were not compelled by a sense of duty to say certain things in order that they might remain in their positions.
Having made those remarks, let me say it is the duty of all members of this house to examine very closely the evidence given by those honourable gentlemen who appeared before the committee. Admiral Landymore presented two very excellent briefs. He was torn between the conditions of his service and the resentful position he was put in by the minister. Whether he liked it or not he found himself in the spotlight of a mounting quarrel.
None can doubt Admiral Landymore's excellent service to this nation over the years. Certainly his promotions over the years to the position he held in the navy, together with the evidence of other people as to his military ability and the way he handled himself before the committee, bear testimony to his integrity. I am sure we were all impressed by his general demeanour and bearing during the time he appeared before the committee.
Admiral Landymore and many other witnesses made a clear distinction between integration and unification, and this brings me to the second point I wish to touch upon. Perhaps I will go into it in detail on another occasion, but at this time I will indicate the nature of this point. The committee in considering this bill, must clearly understand that integration is one thing and unification is another. Unification is another entirely different concept, and until we learn to distinguish between the two we cannot properly understand this legislation.

I am glad the hon. member has withdrawn the allegation or the implications of the remarks he made. I might point out to the hon. member that the so-called contradictions which he mentions as between the evidence given by General Moncel and that given by Air Chief Marshal Miller are not in actual fact contradictions at all.
General Moncel said he had prepared four plans. Air Chief Marshal Miller did not for a moment say General Moncel had not prepared four plans; he merely said they had not come to his attention. This is a different thing altogether. In so far as the estimate of the number of people that would be required is concerned, General Moncel gave his opinion of the size and cost of the force necessary to meet our international commitments. Mr. Chairman, one of the starting points of the integration and unification program of the Canadian armed forces is the creation of a distinctively Canadian force.
Canada is a young country. In the past we have had the good fortune of obtaining from our founding nations all sorts of information and knowledge which have accumulated through the centuries. But, in the life of every nation there comes a time when things past are no longer suitable or sufficient, where the umbilical cord must be severed. Our armed forces are one aspect of our foreign policy, and our foreign policy differs from that of other countries in the word. So why should this not be reflected by our armed forces?
In the last few years Canada has proved great efficiency through its contribution to maintaining peace and order in the word. This was made possible through our participation to alliances and peace keeping operations. We have examples of such operations in places like Suez, Cyprus, Yemen, Kashmir and the Congo.
As our country grew, particular interests and new requirements developed. Canada acquired a unique gratitude almost everywhere in the world. African, Asian and South American peoples know that we have no territorial ambition and that our only interest, in wanting to keep the peace, is to offer an opportunity to men of goodwill to work toward the solution of the problems of sickness, poverty and illiteracy facing humanity.

collectively organized at the level where people can work together. When the minister introduced his bill I wondered whether some of the experiences of the past had been analysed sufficiently. The three forces worked very well together, and I imagine that today there is a projection of this scheme in the battles being fought in Viet Nam. With the rapid changes being made in the conventional type of fighting, I wonder whether it would not be a good idea to have an observer in Viet Nam at the present time? This might, of course, violate Canada's role in so far as the truce team is concerned but certainly with so much at stake it would seem that the experience Canada might gain through having an observer on the fighting lines would be of the greatest importance when we are in the process of changing the structure of our forces.

As one who has tried to keep in contact with the forces during the past few years, I can say honestly that I have found all this talk of integration is welcomed. I can recall visiting some of the forces, various branches of the army and navy, and there was no conflict at all. On the other hand, I sometimes wonder about the position of all those officers who are forced into new positions and who are at the same time giving advice to officers under them. We know certain hypothetical circumstances cannot be foreseen with mathematical precision, but if the action we propose
National Defence Act Amendment through this measure is based on the evidence of those who are competent in military matters, who apply their knowledge to our needs in our relations with other countries, I feel we can say that we are adopting a progressive measure.
Of course, Mr. Chairman, this is not new. Since the beginning of time, upheavals have led to change. Let the students of history recall, for instance, how when cross-bows, arrows and spears were replaced by the blunderbuss, by firearms, one would have thought the world was coming to an end. Of course, parliaments in those days did not have as today transcriptions systems to enable the citizens to read in the archives of the heartbreak of those who opposed the change. But history ever repeats itself.
For instance, when the decision to abandon the cavalry was taken, some generals and marshals threw their uniforms away and resigned from the army, with tears in their eyes, their hearts broken, because they realized that another era was disappearing. Periodic evolution is the most normal thing since the beginning of the world.
When the Maginot line was invented, for instance, and troops were forced to dig themselves in like rats, it was such a novel method that governments were brought down. It proved efficient for a time, and then they came up with mechanized war. In fact, one remembers what trouble General de Gaulle stirred up when he tried to explain to a great number of his colleagues, French officers and parliamentarians, how much mechanized war was a necessity. It took him years, and there again governments were defeated. The world finally accepted what was evident, that mechanized war was a must, something essential.
The same thing happened in the field of aviation, Mr. Chairman. Indeed, it is said that Marshal Petain himself did not believe that aviation could be efficient, and this gave rise to homeric debates in the French parliament of that time.
We have the same process today, except that the revolution is deeper. This is the age of nuclear or atomic war; we are in the age of electronics to the extreme and we must give the Canadian army people whose competence will exceed everything we have imagined to date. We will have to co-ordinate the services, to unify them into a central administration, if our armed forces are to give maximum efficiency.
It seems to me that it is obvious, Mr. Chairman, and it seems to me also that those
April 7, 1967

National Defence Act Amendment who oppose the bill are dead set against it. In any case, even if those who oppose the bill are convinced that some things are not as they should be, why prolong the debate? Everyone knows that the government will introduce the bill as amended. Everyone knows also that some opposition members will oppose it. Everyone will know what the score is when a vote has been held on the matter. Let us take it as quickly as possible and go on to something more constructive.
Some basic truths should be recalled. The government is there to govern. It must govern. And to govern it must decide what legislation is called for. It comes to an opinion after hearing its experts, its department heads, also the opposition. It seems to me that it has been listening to the latter with great patience but, sooner or later, it must decide that the debate has been going on long enough and put a stop to it. I feel that enough has been said on that matter. Parliament speaks, it is the right of parliament to discuss and that of the opposition to oppose, but the debate must end, especially when it is obvious that it does not lead anywhere.
I do not think that deep down any opposition member feels that at this stage of the proceedings he will be able to bring the government to agree to any major amendment, except possibly on some details, when the bill is considered clause by clause.
Mr. Chairman, if the government is making a mistake, after getting advice from all its experts, after reading the evidence for or against the measure, after taking into consideration advice given freely by the opposition, there is a tribunal to which it will be accountable in the years to come. The electorate is, in short, the court of last resort.
Now we have told the government everything we had to tell them, I think it would be only fair to let the government implement its legislation.
Moreover, I do not think we are asked to implement unification overnight. It seems that this process which began spontaneously before the passing of any legislation, simply by the pressure of things, some time after the last war, and which unfolded itself normally, will have to go on unfolding itself and will not be completed before five, six, seven, eight or ten years.

Personally I am not under any obligation to any party, to anyone in this house. I must say that I respect most members of this house, at least those I know, and among them, to a high degree, the Minister of National Defence. I admire his frankness, his honesty, his firmness and his patience in spite of all the criticism heaped on him for many weeks.

If I rose today, Mr. Chairman, it was to appeal to all men of goodwill in this house. As a matter of fact, I know that all men of goodwill realize that everything worthwhile has already been said and that not one iota will be changed by extending the debate for hours and days. On the other hand, this will simply help to discredit Parliament a little more in the eyes of the public, at a time when it has managed to rehabilitate itself somewhat through the constructive work done in the last few months.
Even the opposition has been doing constructive work these last few months. Parliament has been rising in the esteem of the public. We should not destroy these achievements by interminable discussions, personal attacks and theories built on perhaps doubtful competence.
As we were saying, now that everything has been said, let us act, let us vote, and the electorate will judge whether this government is right or wrong.

abilities. I fully agree with the view expressed by the hon. member for Carleton in that the name has been an inconvenience. It is true that the word "secretary" has certain connotations in the United Kingdom which it has never enjoyed in Canada. Indeed, upon my appointment as parliamentary secretary I received a number of letters of congratulation upon my stepping out of politics into the civil service. Some people thought I would never have to go through the rigours of a political contest again. The name certainly has been a cause of confusion. Many people misunderstand what the office is. speechtext:
I would agree with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) that in the centennial year there are grounds for greater co-operation and that when the house is presented with an opportunity, as it was a moment ago, to do something constructive which is recognized on both sides as having merit, it is regrettable we do not seem to have the stuff necessary to do it. As a new member of parliament and, no doubt, an inexperienced one, I think this is regrettable.
The hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Bell) presented cogently and at times movingly a compelling argument for improving the status and the role of parliamentary secretaries. I cannot but concur in the argument he presented on behalf of this bill. The practice in Canada has been that parliamentary secretaries or assistants are not junior ministers as is the case in Britain. Their roles are determined largely by the ministers themselves and necessarily vary from one ministry to another. If I felt that a change of title would lead to an improvement in the status I would agree wholeheartedly with the hon. member for Carleton.
If the words which the hon. member quoted from our late distinguished prime minister, Mackenzie King, were put into practice by ministers there is no doubt that the role of parliamentary secretary could become a more useful and positive one both in government and in the House of Commons. We shall not bring this about simply by increasing the numbers of parliamentary secretaries. I object to the provision which speaks of 16 and envisages possible changes in the future.
This is a role which has to be examined. At present it is something of a no-man's-land. It is not clearly defined and, as I said earlier, it seems to vary from department to department depending on the particular portfolio to
April 7, 1967	COMMONS
which a parliamentary secretary is attached. My main point is that the role of parliamentary secretary or assistant has not been developed as fully as it should be. Every minister needs a parliamentary assistant and I cannot think of one good reason why any minister should refuse one. The responsibilities which ministers of the Crown presently bear must really be back-breaking and there are areas in which a parliamentary assistant could clearly be of help.
What are those areas? I was surprised to learn of some of them as put forward by Mr. Mackenzie King, in what I thought was a highly contemporary piece of thinking. Parliamentary assistants could do a lot more in the way of receiving briefs from interested parties and from pressure groups outside government circles. They could also do a great deal in the way of receiving individuals who always seem to want meetings with ministers. If their role were clearly laid down they could serve as effective liaison between members of parliament and their ministers.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
It would be difficult for me to make suggestions about departmental responsibilities which they might assume. I am not familiar enough with what happens in this area to know, but I would think there would be areas where a parliamentary assistant could do some useful work within a department itself.
In respect to duties in the House of Commons it is perfectly clear that what we expect of our ministers today is more than we should reasonably expect in terms of attendance and responsibility. I would suggest it is unrealisitc and inefficient to expect ministers to attend here as well as to administer the large and complex government departments it is their lot to administer. Parliamentary assistants could serve an extremely useful purpose in relieving their ministers of some of the time those ministers are presently required to attend in the house.
In fact I would hope that parliamentary assistants could be charged with the responsibility of piloting through the House of Commons bills which are not of a particularly controversial or political nature. The hon. member for Carleton very rightly expressed the possibilities for apprenticeship that open up in this area. We are all too cognizant of how important that apprenticeship is in preparation for ministerial responsibilities, and particularly for duties within the House of Commons.
Parliamentary Secretaries Act Amendment
In recent years it has been our sorry lot to witness what can be the consequences to individuals who are over-worked or, in some cases, inexperienced when faced with the responsibilities and the challenges posed by becoming members of the front bench in the House of Commons. No one needs to elaborate on that point. No one needs to apportion blame. It is a fact of life of which all of us should be cognizant and about which we should be concerned. Therefore I would see considerable possibilities for parliamentary assistants in the role that I have just described, that of relieving ministers of some of their duties and responsibilities within the House of Commons.
Another area where a parliamentary assistant could do some very useful work, if given the opportunity, is in assuming some of the responsibilities we presently require of ministers outside the House of Commons and outside their departments. I am thinking of official openings, speaking engagements, and the like. These are very important functions which have to be performed. National organizations, and indeed constituency organizations very often like to have ministers present at their annual meetings to discuss departmental policies, and how they relate to those organizations. Parliamentary assistants could do useful work in this regard.
One final area in which they could do some useful work is in the area of long term policy planning within departments. It is not realistic to expect civil servants to be responsible for projecting in what direction a department is to move in the future, and what are the alternatives or options in policy matters. These are things which are a political task and a parliamentary assistant could do some useful work in this regard.
All I would like to say in closing is that I fully support the arguments presented by the hon. member for Carleton. However, I feel that if this bill passes, the authority vested in parliamentary assistants must be made much greater. Not only must a parliamentary assistant appear to have the confidence of his minister, but he must have that confidence. He must have access to confidential papers and to meetings which his minister has with departmental officials. In short, a parliamentary assistant must become the alter ego of his minister.
